idiom_name: java.util.ServiceLoader provider registry on the JVM (reload() clears the cache)
implementation_notes: On the JVM, Kotlin uses the same mediating instance as Java: ServiceLoader.load(CodecFactory::class.java) resolves providers declared in META-INF/services or module `provides` directives, instantiates them lazily and caches what it has loaded, with ServiceLoader.reload() dropping the cache as the re-resolution hook. What replaces the classic structure is the service interface plus the provider configuration files; idiomatic Kotlin additionally hides the raw loader behind a reified inline helper returning List<T>, so call sites never see Class objects. The mechanism is JVM-only: Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS have no equivalent, so multiplatform code needs an explicit registry.
code_sketch:
val loader = ServiceLoader.load(CodecFactory::class.java)
val factory = loader.firstOrNull() ?: error("no CodecFactory provider")   // name -> provider
val encoder = factory.getEncoder("PNG")
loader.reload()                                                          // re-resolve
pitfalls: An empty ServiceLoader is not an error - code that requires a provider must fail fast itself (firstOrNull() plus an explicit error), otherwise the miss becomes wrong behaviour later.
ServiceConfigurationError is thrown lazily while iterating and is an Error, not an Exception, so a bare catch (e: Exception) never sees it.
Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS have no ServiceLoader; keep JVM provider discovery out of common code.

variants.name: Koin container lookup (get<T>() / by inject())
variants.idiom_name: Koin module declarations plus get<T>() / by inject()
variants.implementation_notes: Koin is the Kotlin-native realization: module { single<Renderer> { HtmlRenderer() } } declarations are the bindings, startKoin installs the container and clients resolve with get<T>() or by inject(), while loadKoinModules() adds bindings at runtime (the closest thing to registration). The lookup is type-keyed, so the 'name' is the resolved type and the binding table is the module graph; because Koin can only be started once, re-resolution means loading or unloading modules rather than restarting the graph. Prefer it for whole-application wiring on Kotlin/JVM, Android and Ktor; prefer ServiceLoader when the bindings must come from third-party jars you do not control.
pitfalls: get<T>() fails only when the graph is used (NoDefinitionFoundException), so a missing binding surfaces at runtime; resolve critical singletons at startup to fail fast.
Type-keyed lookup has no string names, so two bindings of the same type need qualifiers - without them the override wins silently.
Global contexts make tests share state; use koinApplication { } or clear the global context to isolate them.
